George Washington’s Thanksgiving Proclamation in 1789:

"By the President of the United States…

Whereas it is the duty of all Nations to acknowledge the providence of Almighty God, to obey his will, to be grateful for his benefits, and humbly to implore his protection and favor— and whereas both Houses of Congress have by their joint Committee requested me to ‘recommend to the People of the United States a day of public thanksgiving and prayer to be observed by acknowledging with grateful hearts the many signal favors of Almighty God especially by affording them an opportunity peaceably to establish a form of government for their safety and happiness.’

Therefore, I do recommend and assign Thursday the 26th day of November next to be devoted by the People of these States to the service of that great and glorious Being, who is the beneficent Author of all the good that was, that is, or that will be.

May we all unite in rendering unto him our sincere and humble thanks— for his kind care and protection of the People of this Country previous to their becoming a Nation— for the signal and manifold mercies, and the favorable interpositions of his Providence which we experienced in the course and conclusion of the late war— for the great degree of tranquillity, union, and plenty, which we have since enjoyed— for the peaceable and rational manner, in which we have been enabled to establish constitutions of government for our safety and happiness, and particularly the national One now lately instituted— for the civil and religious liberty with which we are blessed; and the means we have of acquiring and diffusing useful knowledge; and in general for all the great and various favors which he hath been pleased to confer upon us.

And also that we may then unite in most humbly offering our prayers and supplications to the great Lord and Ruler of Nations to render our national government a blessing to all the people, by constantly being a Government of wise, just, and constitutional laws, discreetly and faithfully executed and obeyed— to promote the knowledge and practice of true religion and virtue, and the encrease of science among them and us— and generally to grant unto all Mankind such a degree of temporal prosperity as he alone knows to be best.

Under my hand at the City of New-York, 3rd of October in the year of our Lord 1789."

Inflationary is intensifying in Japan:

Japan’s Services Producer Price Index (SPPI) jumped +4.2% YoY in October, its largest annual increase since 1990, and far above expectations of +3.6%.

This index tracks domestic prices businesses charge each other for services, and serves as a key inflation metric in Japan.

MoM, the index rose +1.1%, up from +0.3% in the previous month and marking its biggest monthly increase in 6 months.

The latest surge was driven particularly by higher ocean freight transportation costs, leasing costs, and hotel charges.

Prices in transport and postal activities alone jumped +9.4% YoY in October, following an +8.4% increase in September.

Rising inflationary pressures are strengthening the case for a December rate hike by the Bank of Japan.

BREAKING: US new home sales jumped +14.2% MoM in October, to an annualized rate of 701,000 units, the highest since December 2025, crushing expectations of a -3.8% decline.

This marks the largest monthly increase since November 2025 and the 2nd-largest since August 2022.

It also marks a sharp recovery from the -9.7% MoM decline in September.

October's surge was driven by sales in the South, the nation's largest home-selling region, which soared +36.2% MoM, to an annualized rate of 515,000 units, the highest since March 2021.

At the same time, the median new home sale price fell -0.3% MoM and -3.2% YoY, to $391,300, the 2nd-lowest reading since July 2021.

Since the October 2022 peak, the median new home sale price has declined by $69,000, or -15.0%.

New home prices are falling sharply.

tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
if you're wondering which university to attend to maximize your chances of getting into @ycombinator or @speedrun, here's the chart you've been looking for.

i've researched every startup across the 2026 cohorts of both accelerators and collected data on where their founders studied.

in total, the dataset covers 855 YC startups, 138 a16z speedrun startups and 1,968 founders.

the ranking features the top 50 universities by number of founders. 62% of them are in the US.

of course, accelerators don't accept you simply because of where you studied. but when reviewing thousands of applications, they need a quick way to identify exceptional people, and your educational background is one of the clearest signals.

getting into Harvard and achieving something notable while you're there already says a lot about your abilities. the university has essentially done part of the due diligence and put its reputation behind you.

but not attending one of these universities doesn't mean you're any less capable. there are another 431 universities in the dataset represented by just one founder each. exceptional people can come from anywhere. the best way to show your potential is through achievements that are easy to verify and hard to ignore.

Dear solo founders, I have some reality check data for you.

It's fun to build things with Claude – but you keep forgetting that you will need to land your first users later.

Now follow my math for B2B SaaS – though the principle is the same in other niches:

1 user from Google ads = $300–$750
1 user from LinkedIn = $150-$450
1 user avg paid plan = $50

Bad news though – costs per user above are BOTH paid and free plan users.

So paid = too expensive.
Organic = too long.

And now the reality check:
Would you start a B2B SaaS knowing you might go 9–12 months without a salary?

tweets.text:
Crypto sentiment is about as bad as I can remember jusdging by how much off ramping and quitting I've seen, even amongst close multi cycle friends (I still suspect they will return once better conditions appear). 

FTX was a major CEX going down, which was terrible, but crypto has always recovered from exchanges going down, and many smart people I knew felt the same. 

Covid crash was 0-1 correlation event for everything, which wasn't crypto specific, so it only took a few days for a lot of people to realise, "oh this is probably a good buy" + we had so much tech still to look forward to at that point, as crypto hadn't shipped anything but whitepapers. 

This moment has nasty everything can break type overhang (AI + quantum) + the ghosts of all the past failures and how much stuff hasn't come to fruition. However, it is always very bleak cyclically at this exact quarter every four years. Maybe it is a tad more bleak because we have broken the spirit of so many individuals that believed crypto would become more than fintech, alongside horrible security risk that feels more intense than ever before. I have acted myself on those security fears, so I'm not going to pretend it hasn't affected me. 

The overhang we have here isn't the easiest to move past, like FTX and covid was. 

My base expectation is that 2027 acts similar to 2019 where nothing really happens, more people quit, and AI keeps progressing, but by the end of the year gets to the point where suddenly people look at the crypto protocols that survived and say "oh, this stuff is actually pretty secure". Maybe some new security standards appear, some joint efforts, who knows. 

At the same time from a macro point of view by the middle of 2027 we are past the hiking cycle, and will have more supportive liquidity regime, and all of the bearish crypto narratives will start to melt away as prices recover, and those bearish narratives may eventually become strengths by eoy. 

The bottom will be in well before this. Latest probably January, which would probably fuck the most people up, due to it being later than anticipated. Prices remain good here if you look ahead 6-12 months, but can get really good in the next 6 weeks possibly. I am watching gold for a clearer signal of a bottom, as it likely bottoms first. 

The stock market can only go down so much before you get the reactive function of the Fed. I remain in the camp that true market crashes are no longer tolerated, and the tools that exist to stop that will be deployed. 

Now, prices won't recover for many things (they never do, dispersion will be even bigger), but we will have good returns for the protocols that generate revenue, and Bitcoin will inflect with liquidity (tbc if that inflection is stronger or weaker than previous cycles). Theoretically, liquidity could be a lot better this cycle as the AI buildout is not allowed to fail, and that will be propped up, and needs to be propped up as it is highly unlikely the numbers are going to make sense and meet the lofty expectations in the short term. 

Don't be bullish on dumb crypto stuff. Crypto is not the frontier it once was, but tokenization and better financial rails are real, and that will continue to be a driver of volumes, fees and onboarding (tradfi) for the next few years. 

There will always be a base level of demand for non sovereign assets, which will be dialed up and down based on liquidity, so don't succumb to the Bitcoin is dead forever bottom of the bear market type fud for the nth time. 

I would still keep an eye on the intersection of AI and crypto, as my gut still says that is where something meaningful/interesting happens/continues to happen going forward.

Due to how many assets are going to be available onchain, it makes sense to widen your horizons and upskill yourself using what you have learned from crypto as a jumping off point rather than a "I think I know how to trade all markets" type arrogance. Use this time now to explore other asset classes, and assets you may be interested in. 

Be patient, you have time. There will be signals when we are more likely entering a risk on market regime again.

ZEC with a broken parabola now. Funny how it is always a front page newspaper/magazine that coincides with a big instant sell off. 

$850 the next logical HTF support and will see if it can base there and start to build some support. If it can't then a test of previous ATH (~$750). Will need to do a prolonged period of sideways action for HTF emas/mas to catch up, and that is the bullish case. Maybe I'm wrong, but this is how I see it.

I still think new highs come this cycle (this could be 28/29 tho, unlikely to be an outperformer in 27), but you have to deal with a broken parabola now. You can't have big up without big down. The large unrealised P&L needs to be digested. 

Part of becoming good money is that you need to show there is demand over time, creating belief and demonstrating that the asset bounces back and is anti fragile. There is no avoiding this. 

If you are actually a believer in ZEC and private money thesis then its a very long hold, and this shouldn't particularly bother you. In fact, it should be accepted as an inevitability. The only way to survive something like ZEC long term is sizing it appropriately. No different to BTC in that regard, which is something very few managed.

THE DAILY METALS PULSE ⚡ | NOV 26, 2026  
#Uranium #Silver #Gold #Copper

Brent started the week below $90 and settled Thanksgiving at $96.57. Gold was down 0.4% by evening. Silver was up 0.8%. For metals investors, the question going into Friday is whether the jump in oil shows up in U.S. Treasury yields when New York reopens.

🛢️ Oil rose after the Houthis said they had struck a Saudi refinery and Iran reported mine strikes on ships in the Strait of Hormuz. The extent of any supply disruption remains uncertain. With U.S. core PCE inflation already at 3.3%, a sustained rise in crude would give the Fed another reason to keep policy tight.

🥈 Silver traded at $41.54/oz by 19:01 GMT, holding above $41 after slipping back from $41.88 in Asia. Gold eased to $3,567/oz. Silver kept more of its early strength even as gold gave up its morning gain.

🔌 Copper briefly reclaimed $12,000 a tonne on the London Metal Exchange, reaching $12,089. One detail in Washington’s tariff proposal helped explain the relief. The proposed duties on 14 trading partners would replace the July rates where they apply. Importers had faced the prospect of paying both.

☢️ Toronto offered a look at uranium sentiment while U.S. equities were closed. The Global X Uranium Index ETF was up 3.8% at C$35.00 by 3:30 p.m. ET. Platts resumes its U₃O₈ price assessments on Monday, so Friday’s U.S. session will give us another read on uranium equities before the next Platts fuel price.

Friday’s U.S. equity session ends at 1 p.m. ET. My first look will be at the two-year Treasury yield. If it climbs and silver can still clear $42, that would tell me more about buying interest than a move through $42 on holiday volume alone.

Follow @Swedish_Uranium for the next Daily Metals Pulse.

$HGRAF $HG.CN #Graphene #Cement

How much of the world’s cement would have to contain HydroGraph graphene for the stock to go 100×? Using the assumptions in my table below, I get just under 3%. That gives plastics, coatings, batteries and defense a combined value of zero.

The number worth revisiting is US$250/kg. CEO Kjirstin Breure has discussed that low end of pricing for large bulk orders of HydroGraph’s fractal graphene. Cement is exactly where I’d use it. A precast producer buying the same additive by the tonne has every reason to negotiate the best bulk price. A customer buying a specialty formulation with HydroGraph’s IP is a different sale.

So why would a concrete producer pay even US$250/kg? At a dosage tested by Arizona State researchers, one tonne of cement takes just 200 grams of graphene. That’s US$50. Lab tests on mortar showed early compressive strength gains of up to 70%. For a precast plant, the question is whether getting a beam out of its mold sooner lets it cast more beams per week. That’s a benefit a plant manager can put a dollar figure on.

Now take that 200-gram dose to a market that produced 3.8 BILLION tonnes of cement in 2025. If HydroGraph supplied the graphene going into 3% of that output, the annual numbers would be:

• 114 million tonnes of cement treated
• 22,800 tonnes of dry graphene sold
• US$5.7 billion in revenue at US$250/kg
• Just under US$3 billion in earnings at my modeled 52.5% net margin

My original 20,000-tonne row worked out to C$362.25/share at 40× earnings. Extend that same row to 22,800 tonnes, keep the same 400 million diluted shares and exchange rate, and I get C$413/share. Against the November 25 close of C$4.00, that’s roughly 103×.
tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
$HGRAF #Uranium #Silver #Gold #Graphene

Why I keep a potential 100× outcome on the table for HydroGraph and have made it my biggest bet ever: exceptional margins combined with production capacity that can be replicated.

The attached table puts numbers behind that possibility.

At an assumed selling price of US$250/kg, selling 10,000 tonnes annually would generate US$2.5 BILLION in revenue. US$250/kg is the minimum price, in most cases it will be much higher.

Start with an assumed 80% gross margin. Deduct operating expenses equal to 10% of revenue, then apply 25% tax. That leaves a 52.5% net margin and approximately US$1.31 billion in annual earnings.

Using 400 million diluted shares and US$1 = C$1.38:

• 5,000 tonnes at P/E 30 → C$67.92/share. • 10,000 tonnes at P/E 30 → C$135.84/share. • 20,000 tonnes at P/E 40 → C$362.25/share.

These are conditional future valuations, not price targets. The assumptions are shown in the table.

For perspective, an 80% margin AFTER all-in sustaining costs would require roughly $9,650 gold, $117 silver or $300 uranium, using respective costs of $1,930/oz, $23.44/oz and an ASSUMED $60/lb. That is a different, stricter measure than HydroGraph’s prospective gross margin.

That creates a compelling possibility: growing volumes, strong earnings and expansion increasingly funded internally.

The opportunity spans coatings, polymers, concrete and defense. Successful adoption across several of those markets could support a business far larger than the first Texas facility.

$HGRAF $HG.CN #Graphene #Cement

How much of the world’s cement would have to contain HydroGraph graphene for the stock to go 100×? Using the assumptions in my table below, I get just under 3%. That gives plastics, coatings, batteries and defense a combined value of zero.

The number worth revisiting is US$250/kg. CEO Kjirstin Breure has discussed that low end of pricing for large bulk orders of HydroGraph’s fractal graphene. Cement is exactly where I’d use it. A precast producer buying the same additive by the tonne has every reason to negotiate the best bulk price. A customer buying a specialty formulation with HydroGraph’s IP is a different sale.

So why would a concrete producer pay even US$250/kg? At a dosage tested by Arizona State researchers, one tonne of cement takes just 200 grams of graphene. That’s US$50. Lab tests on mortar showed early compressive strength gains of up to 70%. For a precast plant, the question is whether getting a beam out of its mold sooner lets it cast more beams per week. That’s a benefit a plant manager can put a dollar figure on.

Now take that 200-gram dose to a market that produced 3.8 BILLION tonnes of cement in 2025. If HydroGraph supplied the graphene going into 3% of that output, the annual numbers would be:

• 114 million tonnes of cement treated
• 22,800 tonnes of dry graphene sold
• US$5.7 billion in revenue at US$250/kg
• Just under US$3 billion in earnings at my modeled 52.5% net margin

My original 20,000-tonne row worked out to C$362.25/share at 40× earnings. Extend that same row to 22,800 tonnes, keep the same 400 million diluted shares and exchange rate, and I get C$413/share. Against the November 25 close of C$4.00, that’s roughly 103×.

$SYH.V $SYHBF $DNN #Uranium

How many shares would a junior uranium explorer have to issue to put C$40 million into the ground? Skyharbour has given Denison Mines a reason to write those cheques itself.

At Wheeler North and Getty East, Denison has committed to at least C$4 million of exploration in the first two years. To earn 70% of both projects, it would spend C$25 million at Wheeler North and C$15 million at Getty East over seven years, plus pay Skyharbour C$3.5 million in cash. Even after both full earn-ins, Skyharbour would own 30% of each.

The drills are already part of the story. Denison reported 1,915 metres drilled at Wheeler North by the end of September. In October, Skyharbour started a Denison-funded program at Getty East targeting another 3,600 metres.

Across the basin at Preston, Orano Canada had already spent C$4.8 million on the project by the time it earned its initial majority stake in 2021. The Orano-led team drilled 5,565 metres in 2025. Its 2026 plan called for an airborne gravity survey and up to 3,500 metres of follow-up drilling. Skyharbour retains 20.8%.

Here’s why I’m bullish on that structure. When a junior sells shares to fund a drill program, existing shareholders give up a slice of every discovery the company might ever make. Denison earns its larger stake on two specific properties. Orano’s stake is at Preston. Neither deal touches Skyharbour’s 100% ownership of Moore.

A discovery at any one of those partner projects could change what Skyharbour is worth. Meanwhile, it can put its own exploration dollars into Moore and its 80%-owned RL claims. As a shareholder, I like having several ways to win without having to fund every hole.

Disclosure: Paid partnership with Skyharbour Resources.

One of the easiest real time metrics to track for @silencioNetwork is Raffle Tickets Activity, which has been accelerating rapidly since June this year, with November already setting a new monthly ATH.

More tickets means more users contributing recordings to the dataset and many of these contributions likely come from newer languages, which often receive ticket boosts. The bigger the quantity and breadth of quality recordings, the more valuable this dataset becomes to AI labs.

Some napkin math. One way to estimate revenue would be to divide quarterly revenue by the cumulative tickets generated up to each quarter, as the dataset grows. Here you can observe that revenue earned per cumulative ticket increased from Q1 through Q3, reflecting the growing monetization of the dataset.

Even if you use the average revenue per cumulative ticket across the first three quarters and apply that to Q4's projected cumulative ticket count, based on the current activity, that would put Q4 revenue at around $1.05M.

Q4 ticket activity itself is on track to be roughly 3x Q3.

This estimate is also in line with the team's forecast and brings full-year revenue to approximately $2.1M. At a 75% buyback rate, Q4 revenue alone could translate to around $790K in token purchases, assuming the initial revenue buffer has already been met.

That's roughly 6% of the current $13M market cap in a single quarter.

I have some bittersweet news to share. After over 5 years, I have made the difficult decision to sunset ZenAcademy and The 333 Club.

I shared a full announcement in Discord yesterday with some in-depth thoughts, so will share screenshots of those below.

Thank you to everyone who played any part in our journey. From team members, to community members, to partners we worked with, and everyone else.

I'm immensely proud of the work we did. We helped educate tens of thousands of people worldwide about NFTs, crypto, and later AI.

We worked with governments and universities, we worked with companies of all sizes, and we gave out almost all of our content for free.

We spoke at dozens of conferences globally and had dozens of meetups.

We provided 1:1 lifecoaching through our ZenCoaching program to ~100 individuals.

We supported dozens of artists via our Zenmas programs.

I personally held over 1000 hours of 1:1 calls with 333 club members.

I got married last year and over 25% of the wedding list were members of ZenAcademy. Kind of a crazy thing to think about.

I'm sorry that there wasn't a better ending to it all, but I tried my best at trying my best.

I don't know what's next for me. Earlier this week I made my newsletter fully free to all again. I will be taking some time and space to think about what life has in store for me from here.

From the bottom of my heart, especially to anyone who ever called ZenAcademy home: thank you.

Roy / Zeneca

But here is the thing about macro: EVERYTHING is a probability-weighted game. You put the odds on scenarios, you size for them, and then the world changes the odds on you. It happens all the time, and it will make you wrong from time to time. That is not a bug in the process. That is the process.

Anyone who tells you they avoid drawdowns, or that they are never wrong, is not worth listening to. They are either not taking risk, or not telling you the truth.

I don't have perma views. I am not a perma bull or a perma bear on anything. I let my own data guide me, the nowcasts I built to track growth, inflation and liquidity in real time, and our in-sample testing of them is very strong. The goal is not to be right every month. It is to be more right than wrong over time, and to know when the data has changed its mind before the market has.

Right now that data is telling me something very different from what the Fed was handed this week.

🚨NEW EPISODE🚨

Last Thurs, Joachim Klement – Head of Strategy at @PanmureLiberum – issued a bold note titled
“This Is It: Why I’m Selling”.

He then sold all his equities. It was a great short term call, will it be long term? He joined me yesterday, six days on from the call to test his thesis:

- “I think that we are heading towards a major bear market with more than 30% drawdown risk”
- Falling below 200 day moving average was the key trigger
- Why 200dma isn’t always great timing tool, but why he’s putting so much behind it this time
- Why the bounce on Monday that failed to regain the 200dma has strengthened his conviction
- Key dates and levels to watch from here for SP500 and 200dma
- “You cannot ignore price momentum. No matter how much of a value guy you are, you can't just stand on the tracks and see a train coming towards you and say, 'well, eventually that train has to stop.' Yeah, eventually it has, but until then you could be dead.”
- AI capex growth slowing
- Anthropic revenue growth slowing
- Analyst estimates still complacently confident
- “So my conviction that AI is a bubble is the highest that I've had any conviction in the last 30 years. The question about when is it going to burst…is that it will burst either in 2027 or 2028. And over the last week or two I think if you want to put it on a scale from 1 to 10, my conviction is a 7 or 8, that it is going to burst now or in early 2027.”

I am a bit of a sucker for books about Wall Street, particularly when I know some of the people. I finally finished Money to Burn, in part a biography of Leon Black as well as the story of Apollo. 

It comes across as an honest storytelling. There is a lot to be learned here about business building, investing, private credit, and the struggle for power that inevitably seems to characterize investment firms. 

It has some Epstein, a few affairs, and other good stuff to make it movie-worthy. 

If you are into Wall Street and investing, this one is not to be missed.

Have we seen the bottom? We will only know in hindsight. None of us will time it correctly.

But these are definitely tradable bottoms. When the Nasdaq is already down 16% and opens another 4% lower for no apparent reason, you have to be buying something.

If you read my 2025 year-end review and outlook for 2026, I expected low to negative returns from the Nasdaq for the very same reason I believe it will rise meaningfully in 2027.

2026 is the year of AI infrastructure investment. I believe 2027 is when the hyperscalers will start monetizing those investments and generating meaningful profits.

My shopping list for 2027 is as follows:

First tier: $AMZN, $SPCX, $META

Second tier: $GOOG, $MSFT, $NVDA

Third tier (speculative): $ORCL
tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
Keep cool. This too shall pass.

Tech earnings may not be entirely sustainable, but when technology companies trade well below their historical multiples, with some trading at just 3x earnings, you have a substantial margin of safety even if those earnings are overstated.

Right now, the market seems to be treating the entire tech sector as one giant fraud.

There have been very few instances in recent history when selling into this level of fear would have left you better off 12 months later. One of them was the GFC, when the financial system itself was on the verge of collapse.

Many of the companies I am looking at today offer a valuation cushion that simply wasn’t there going into the GFC.

Hold the line.

SPX average returns 12 month out below.

tweets.text:
𝗛𝗢𝗪 𝗗𝗢𝗘𝗦 𝗦𝗧𝗔𝗡𝗟𝗘𝗬 𝗗𝗥𝗨𝗖𝗞𝗘𝗡𝗠𝗜𝗟𝗟𝗘𝗥 𝗨𝗦𝗘 𝗖𝗛𝗔𝗥𝗧𝗦?

Over the past couple of days, I analyzed how Stanley Druckenmiller, one of the greatest investors of all time, uses charts in his investment process.

What I found fascinating is that in the interviews I reviewed, you won’t find any of the crap you see on X from subscription sellers drawing cups and handles, Fibonacci retracements, support and resistance lines, and all sorts of imaginary formations.

He looks for essentially the same things I look for in a chart.

𝟭. 𝗖𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲𝘀 𝗶𝗻 𝗠𝗼𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘂𝗺

In his 2009 interview with Jeff Feig, Druckenmiller explained that his proprietary charting system uses a “second-derivative rate of change.”

He looks at changes in momentum that may precede changes in fundamentals, rather than trying to predict prices based on geometric formations.

𝟮. 𝗣𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗲 𝗔𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗥𝗲𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝗡𝗲𝘄𝘀

In his 2023 interview with Nicolai Tangen:

“A big part of my process is price action versus news.”

How does a stock behave following bad news? Does it recover from a significant selloff? Does it refuse to appreciate despite improving fundamentals?

Interestingly, he also acknowledges that this approach has become less reliable because of algorithmic trading and increased competition.

𝟯. 𝗠𝗮𝗿𝗸𝗲𝘁 𝗕𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗱𝘁𝗵 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗟𝗶𝗾𝘂𝗶𝗱𝗶𝘁𝘆

In his 1992 interview with Jack Schwager for The New Market Wizards:

“I never use valuation to time the market. I use liquidity considerations and technical analysis for timing.”

He looks at whether the broader market is participating in a rally or whether a handful of large companies are masking weakness elsewhere.

𝟰. 𝗙𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗮𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗹𝘀 𝗙𝗶𝗿𝘀𝘁

In his 2009 interview, he explained that approximately 75% to 80% of his investment ideas originate from fundamental analysis and that he does not invest solely on the basis of a chart.

𝗜𝗻 𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲, 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗵𝗲 𝗹𝗼𝗼𝗸𝘀 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗶𝘀:

• Changes in momentum.
• Trend reversals.
• Relative strength and weakness.
• Price action in response to news.
• Market breadth.
• Liquidity conditions.

A chart is a record of market behavior, not a crystal ball.

Avoid the noise, ignore the imaginary formations, and focus on what truly matters.

Without sounding egotistical, I genuinely believe my account is one of the best places to learn how the stock market works.

There are many great investment books, but most describe what worked five, ten, or twenty years ago. Markets constantly evolve. The emergence of algorithmic trading, AI, and new market participants has fundamentally changed market dynamics.

What makes this account different is that you get daily reflections in real time. What I did right, what I did wrong, what worked, what didn’t, and what I could have done better.

I make a conscious effort to examine my own decisions as if I were an outside observer, without letting my ego interfere. I openly acknowledge my mistakes and share my successes, trying to learn equally from both.

Rather than simply reading about how someone navigated the markets twenty years ago, you get to observe an investor navigating today’s market, reflecting on his decisions and constantly adapting.

The purpose of this account is not to show you how good an investor I am, but to help you become a better one.

There are many great investment books, but most describe what worked five, ten, or twenty years ago. Markets constantly evolve. The emergence of algorithmic trading, AI, and new market participants has fundamentally changed market dynamics.

What makes this account different is that you get daily reflections in real time. What I did right, what I did wrong, what worked, what didn’t, and what I could have done better.

I make a conscious effort to examine my own decisions as if I were an outside observer, without letting my ego interfere. I openly acknowledge my mistakes and share my successes, trying to learn equally from both.

Rather than simply reading about how someone navigated the markets twenty years ago, you get to observe an investor navigating today’s market, reflecting on his decisions and constantly adapting.

The purpose of this account is not to show you how good an investor I am, but to help you become a better one.

For long horizon LLM tasks, sometimes you’ll come back after multiple hours of work and have no idea what happened.

That’s expected; it’s akin to being on holiday for a week and coming back to your job.

A dastardly simple fix if you’re lost is to tell the model to zoom out:

Zoom out. Assume I have no prior context and I’m seeing all of this for the first time. Explain what’s going on in simple terms. Narrow it down to the most important findings, decisions, or components, and give me a recommendation with a justification if appropriate. If the decision chain is complex, make me an HTML walkthrough to aid my understanding and decision-making.

The alternative version is: I’ve been hit over the head with a rock and have amnesia, please help.

Underlying theme here is that models can get a lot of useful stuff done autonomously. 

You don’t need to be in the loop to read every message and tool call, especially if the work was properly planned. 

But your judgment is still important, so rather than 1) going full Hail Mary/Jesus take the wheel; or 2) throwing away the work because you can’t immediately follow it, just ask the model to lift the fog. 

It sounds super simple, and it is.

It’s not 2024, you don’t need to be some prompt engineer typing diabolical shit like “You are a 165 IQ genius programmer with a girlfriend who loves him and doesn’t care that his crypto port is down 90%…” 

You can just do things.

Depending on the task, I'll usually do a long voice note dump on what I'm thinking, the requirements, edge cases, what a definition of done looks like and so forth.

Then I will explicitly tell the model that I want this work to be autonomous and ask it for a proposal. I'll usually tell it to include orchestration, i.e. what models to use in what threads, sequencing etc. as part of the proposal.

Then I'll read the proposal and either give feedback or give a simple 'go'.

Permissions mode set to Bypass Permissions (if you're confident/depending on the work and the environment).

The problem with predicting the bottom is that the price is already up by 25% or more.

Based on my dictionary, the bottom is in place if it gives the following sequence

Low, High, higher low, lower high, and finally a new high.
subtle variation
Low, High, higher low, higher-high

Look at $SOXX chart; the sequence that we got is:
Low, High, higher low, lower high, and then lower-low

We are still in the process of a downtrend
And when you are trading counter-trend, you need to be familiar with the rules of engagement

Overnight risk is real; sizing and cushion help navigate

tweets.text:
Pearl = (3,3) for inference providers

Olympus DAO / TIME Wonderland → offers high APR for token stakers (requires buying & staking the tokens) back during 2020-21 cycle

Pearl → high APR for inference providers (no need to buy & stake, inference providers can simultaneously run own inference, earn 100% of inference revenue + PEARL emission)

For the bull case to play out, SoV narrative needs to hold (i.e. people treat PEARL as "AI Inference Money" or "BTC for Inference"), early investors hold amidst 80%+ inflation, price go up as a result

The bear case is simple - inference providers farm and dump, early investors dump, everyone dumps

No matter which way it goes, inference providers are the ultimate beneficiary as they can farm PEARL for a very low overhead 

(no additional cost incurred because they own the GPUs, cost will be even lower when FP8 upgrade comes)

It's been three weeks since this post. Many people, myself included, are incredibly interested in this report, and more specifically, in Anthropic's AL4 number. I was really hoping it would drop this week, but if we don't see it in the next few hours it will probably be next week now at the earliest.

AL4 stands for Automation Level 4, and it's a really strong indicator of how close we are to RSI. It basically means a human dev picks something for Claude to work on, Claude handles the rest end-to-end, and then the human reviews and deploys it. It's the last step before Claude chooses what to work on itself and deploys it itself (AL5), at which point no human is required anymore for model development, though they can still choose to take part. The only speed limit after that is how much compute you have and how many electrons you can pour into it. It's also possible that Anthropic's workflow already contains a small amount of AL5. Speculation abounds.

In February, Anthropic's AL4 was under 1%. By August, it had jumped to 26%. We haven't seen any new numbers since then, and it's now November 26th. This is approximately 700 years in AI time. Naturally, a lot of us want to see how fast that number has climbed.

Sam McCandlish said in a follow-up reply that the reason Anthropic redacted so much of the METR report on their internal acceleration was that 'the unredacted information would allow others to speed up their research.' It's possible the same thinking is behind the delay here. There are many possibilities, one being that if Anthropic's automated research levels really are as high as some people are speculating, it will shock their competitors - making them realize how much is possible and how fast Anthropic is taking off. That would incentivize other labs into pursuing RSI even harder than they already are (difficult to do in some cases), and throwing even more resources at it. Sometimes knowing what's possible is enough.

Still, Christmas is less than a month away. We're now approaching 2027, when many are predicting we reach full RSI, and some even ASI shortly afterward following the resultant acceleration. So it feels like it's past time to let us all know what's going on inside the mysterious Tower of Claude and reveal the current shape of the invisible frontier.
tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
I'm Sam, one of Anthropic's co-founders, and I lead much of our safety work. I'm going to have more to share on that work over the coming months.

I thought I'd start by sharing a few thoughts on the latest report from @METR_Evals.

The speed of progress in model capabilities is one of the most important questions in AI safety, and METR’s work here provides the public with an independent, external view into how this is happening inside Anthropic. I’ll talk more about some of the details below, but first some context for those new to this work.

How quickly AI progress is accelerating has many important safety implications, since it determines how quickly the risks from advanced models increase. But, because most research happens within the frontier labs, it’s difficult for external observers and policy makers to get a strong sense of what that rate is. We kicked off the process with METR that led to this report earlier in the year, in anticipation of progress continuing to accelerate.

For this report, we gave METR access to a range of sensitive internal data, including benchmark scores for unreleased models, estimates of how models are progressing, and interviews with our researchers. They had complete independence to form their own conclusions.

Many of their conclusions match my own. AI is speeding up our research, but it’s hard to say exactly how much. While they conclude AI can't yet make the most important contributions to model training on its own, they think the pace of development could, by default, accelerate further.

This work began well before and is separate from the embedded third-party evaluators that are part of our commitment to pacing the frontier, but it’s a good illustration of why we think evaluators are a good idea. The more access reviewers have, the clearer a picture they can form of the situation and the better-positioned they are to highlight situations like this one.

We redacted a lot, and I accept that this makes it harder for others to check METR’s work. But we determined that sharing exactly what is driving the speedup isn’t the right thing to do, both because it’s commercially sensitive and because it risks handing out a roadmap for others to go faster. That would make the risks METR is worried about worse. That’s a tradeoff. I think we made the right call, though we’re continuing to assess the pros and cons here.

In the coming weeks, we plan to share a report with our own analysis of the speed of AI progress within Anthropic, including where we stand against our Responsible Scaling Policy, plus new steps we’re taking to strengthen our safety and security practices as AI keeps improving quickly.
